description: Track a supply-chain attack — a backdoored dependency, a compromised vendor, a malicious npm/PyPI/cargo/Maven package, a tampered Docker image, or a compromised GitHub Action. Captures the malicious component, affected versions, and downstream impact.
name: Supply chain compromise

structure.help: Headline: which component, which ecosystem, when it surfaced.
structure.label: Compromise overview

structure.help: Name of the package / image / action / vendor product. e.g. *event-stream*, *colors.js*, *codecov-bash*, *3CX Desktop App*. Drives the event info field.
structure.label: Compromised component

structure.help: Short tag for *where the component lives*. e.g. `npm`, `PyPI`, `Maven Central`, `cargo`, `Docker Hub`, `GitHub Actions`, `vendor binary`. Drives the event info field alongside the component name.
structure.label: Ecosystem

structure.help: When you started tracking this — typically the upstream advisory or detection date.
structure.label: Date observed

structure.help: One or two sentences orienting a reader. What got compromised, how was the malice introduced (typosquat / hijacked maintainer / subdomain takeover / build-system breach / hardware), and how was it discovered.
structure.label: Short summary

structure.help: Which versions of the component carry the malicious code. Operators downstream need this to scope their exposure.
structure.label: Affected versions

structure.help: Specific version string carrying the malicious code (e.g. `1.4.18`, `v3.4.0`). Use the **+ Add another instance** for a contiguous-but-bounded range.
structure.label: Affected version

misp.comment_template: Version known to carry the malicious code

structure.help: When the affected versions form a range (e.g. `>= 4.0.0, < 4.0.7`), capture it here free-form rather than enumerating every patch version.
structure.label: Affected version range

structure.help: The version to upgrade to. Strongly preferred over leaving operators to guess.
structure.label: Fixed version

structure.help: Where the malicious component was hosted. Helps downstream tooling block the source.
structure.label: Distribution channel

structure.help: Direct link to the registry entry — e.g. `https://www.npmjs.com/package/<name>`, `https://pypi.org/project/<name>/`, `https://hub.docker.com/r/<org>/<image>`.
structure.label: Package / image URL

structure.help: Upstream source repo (typically GitHub / GitLab). Often distinct from the package URL when the registry is just a build artifact host.
structure.label: Source repository URL

structure.help: Username of the maintainer who pushed the malicious version. For hijacked-account incidents, this is the legitimate-but-compromised account; for typosquats, it's the attacker's freshly-registered alias.
structure.label: Maintainer account

structure.help: What the malicious component actually does on a victim machine.
structure.label: Malicious payload

structure.help: If you have the malicious package / image as a single binary, capture its hashes here. The malware-sample sub-relation gets MISP to encrypt at rest.
structure.label: Malicious artifact (file)

relations.help_override: e.g. `colors-1.4.44-liberty-2.tgz` or the Docker layer digest's tarball name.

structure.help: URL or hostname the malicious code reaches out to. Often only triggers on specific environment markers (CI, prod) — note the trigger condition in the *Behaviour notes* below.
structure.label: C2 / exfil endpoint

structure.help: Free-form. What does the malicious code do, and what triggers it? e.g. *Only fires when CI=true and GITHUB_REPOSITORY contains 'ethereum'*. Crucial for triage scoping.
structure.label: Behaviour notes

structure.help: Upstream advisory, security blog post, vendor incident page.
structure.label: References

structure.help: Vendor / registry advisory, security blog, GitHub Security Advisory entry. One URL per entry.
structure.label: Advisory URL

structure.help: TLP, kill-chain, and any actor / campaign attribution.
structure.label: Classification and attribution

structure.help: Pick one. Most published supply-chain advisories are TLP:WHITE; in-house tracking with internal exposure detail may be tighter.
structure.label: TLP

structure.help: Supply-chain compromises typically fall under *delivery* (the malicious package is the delivery mechanism) or *exploitation* / *installation* depending on what the payload does.
structure.label: Kill chain phase

structure.help: Optional. Many supply-chain incidents are opportunistic; only attribute when the operator has evidence beyond the technique alone.
structure.label: Suspected threat actor

structure.content: **A note on scope:** the *Behaviour notes* field is doing real work here — many supply-chain payloads are environmentally-conditioned (only fire in CI, only target specific git remotes, only trigger after N invocations). Capture the trigger condition; it's what tells downstream readers whether their environment is exposed.
